newsitem.title: USA: Republican tax bill good for women - Dunn.
newsitem.headline: Republican tax bill good for women - Dunn.

text.p: Working women would be the big winners under Republican-proposed tax cuts, Representative Jennifer Dunn of Washington said Saturday.

As White House and congressional negotiators sought to iron out differences in their tax proposals, Dunn used the weekly Republican radio address to declare that the cuts proposed by Congress would help middle-income tax payers more than those proposed by the Clinton administration.
"Middle-income workers are the big winners under our plan," said Dunn. "Helping American families, and especially America's women, is all part of the Republican agenda."
"Under President Clinton's plan, we believe American families are short-changed," said Dunn, who serves on the tax-writing House Ways and Means Committee.

Negotiators met over the weekend to try to work out differences between tax proposals of the White House, the House and Senate, all of which have differences. Both the White House and Republicans insist their plans would give the greatest relief to middle-income taxpayers.
Dunn, who is not directly involved in the talks, did not spell out differences between the tax plans put forth by the House and Senate, both of which are controlled by Republicans.
But she said a Republican proposal to raise the inheritance tax exemption to $1 million from $600,000 could also save trees.

She cited the experience of Helen Anderson of North Bend, Wash., who she said was forced to cut down 60-year old timber on 20 of the 50 acres that she inherited from her parents to pay estate taxes and related costs.

"In the end not a dollar was left," said Dunn. "And 20 acres of beautiful 60-year old timber that had been home to wildlife and a peaceful place for hikers was gone. Estate tax relief will help people like Helen."
While all plans include a version of a $500 per child tax credit, Dunn said the Clinton plan would leave "the typical middle-income family with two children" with less.
She said 76 percent of the Republican tax cuts go to taxpayers making less than $75,000 a year.

The Republican plan will help women with the child credit and with breaks on higher education costs and expanded use of Individual Retirement Accounts, she said. And the proposed capital gains tax cut will help women start their own businesses, including those that allow them to work from home, she added.
Differences between the White House and Republicans remain over the size of higher education tax breaks, an administration priority, and the application of the child tax credit.

On Friday, Republican negotiators, under a self-imposed deadline of the end of next week for crafting a final tax bill, said they took a step toward the White House's position in an effort to "get the ball moving," but declined to elaborate.
The two sides have already agreed to a framework as part of an agreement to balance the budget over five years that includes $85 billion in tax cuts.
